Diazepam: Pfizer. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
Boeing 777X: United States. The Boeing 777X is an American long-range, wide-body, twin-engine airliner built by Boeing Commercial Airplanes, undergoing flight testing.
Who is credited with discovering Microscopium?
Microscopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. The name is a Latinised form of the Greek word for microscope.
Who is credited with discovering Toluene?
Toluene: Pierre Joseph Pelletier. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
Who is credited with discovering Pethidine?
Pethidine: Otto Eisleb. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.
Who is credited with discovering Polonium?
Polonium: Marie Curie. Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.

While working at a Soviet computing centre in 1985, this engineer created one of history's most popular video games — yet earned no royalties from it until founding a company with Henk Rogers in 1996. Who is he?
Alexey Pajitnov (born April 16, 1955) is a Russian and American computer engineer and video game designer.
Multicellular, oxygen-breathing, and all descended from a single common ancestor, this kingdom ranges in size from 8.5 micrometers to 33.6 meters. What is it?
Animal are multicellular, eukaryotic organisms belonging to the biological kingdom Animalia.

Around 1920, when the energy source of stars was a complete mystery, which English astrophysicist boldly and correctly guessed it was the fusion of hydrogen into helium — and lent his name to a natural ceiling on a star's brightness?
Arthur Eddington (28 December 1882 - 22 November 1944) was an English astrophysicist and mathematician.
Native to Europe, this small white-petaled, yellow-centered lawn flower is called 'common,' 'lawn,' or 'English' in various regions — what is its scientific name?
Bellis perennis (p-), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
This leafy vegetable forms no head, just green blades atop pale bulbous stalks, with a flavor often compared to a mix of spinach and water chestnut — what vegetable is it?

Bok choy (American English, Canadian English, and Australian English), pak choi (British English, South African English, and Caribbean English) or pok choi is a type of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp.
Unlike ordinary weight loss from undereating, this illness-linked syndrome strips away muscle mass in ways good nutrition can't fully undo — what condition is it?
Cachexia is a syndrome that occurs in people with certain illnesses, causing muscle loss that cannot be fully reversed with improved nutrition.
This neuropsychiatric syndrome, often linked to mood or psychotic disorders, can leave a person nearly motionless for days or cause repetitive, purposeless movements. What is it?
Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome most commonly seen in people with underlying mood disorders such as major depressive disorder, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.
Native to East Asia and blooming late in the season, these autumn flowers of the daisy family are associated in the Northern Hemisphere with the month of November. What flower is it?
Chrysanthemum (kriss-), sometimes abbreviated to mums or chrysanths, are perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the family Asteraceae that bloom in the autumn.
This highly poisonous member of the carrot family can grow to nearly 8 feet tall, with hollow, maroon-spotted stems and a famously unpleasant odor — what plant is it?
Conium maculatum (British English) or poison hemlock (in North America), is a highly poisonous flowering plant and a nitrophile weed species in the carrot family Apiaceae.
Unrelated to poor hygiene, this scalp condition causes flaking and mild itching and is often treated with antifungal or keratolytic remedies; about half of all adults experience it. What is it?
Dandruff is a skin condition of the scalp. It can result in social or self-esteem problems.
Made from a fermented batter of ground black gram and rice, this thin South Indian bread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar — what is it?

Dosa (food) (in Indian English) or thosai (in Malaysian English and Singapore English) is a thin, savoury batter bread in South Indian cuisine made from a fermented batter of ground black gram and rice.
The tallest native bird in Australia and the third-tallest living bird overall, this flightless ratite can grow up to 1.9 metres tall. What bird is it?
Emu (Dromaius novaehollandiae) is a species of flightless bird endemic to Australia, where it is the tallest native bird.
Equivalent to one coulomb per volt, this SI unit of electrical capacitance is named after a pioneering English physicist — name the unit?
Farad (symbol: F) is the unit of electrical capacitance, the ability of a body to store an electrical charge, in the International System of Units (SI), equivalent to 1 coulomb per volt (C/V).
After working in Feynman's group on the Manhattan Project, this physicist later co-detected a famously elusive elementary particle, winning the 1995 Nobel — who was he?
Frederick Reines (March 16, 1918 - August 26, 1998) was an American physicist.

Encoded by the codons CAA and CAG and structurally related to glutamic acid but with an amide in place of a carboxylic acid group, this charge-neutral amino acid becomes essential under bodily stress — which amino acid?
Glutamine (symbol Gln or Q) is an -amino acid that is used in the biosynthesis of proteins.

Also called the harlequin or multicoloured Asian type, this exceptionally variable insect established itself across Africa and South America after being introduced beyond its native Asia — what species?
Harmonia axyridis is a lady beetle or ladybird species that is most commonly known as the harlequin, Asian, or multicoloured Asian lady beetle.

This broad academic category studies human society, culture, and its fundamental questions — during the Renaissance, the term specifically meant the study of classical literature and language as a secular alternative to religious studies. Name the category?
Humanities are academic disciplines that study aspects of human society and culture, including certain fundamental questions asked by humans.

This pathogen has caused seasonal flu in humans and also infects birds and some mammals; strains circulate constantly in bats, pigs, horses, and dogs. It was the cause of the Spanish Flu pandemic from 1918 to 1920. What is it?
Influenza A virus is a pathogen with strains that cause seasonal flu in humans; it can also infect birds and some mammals.

Called 'the greatest investor on Wall Street,' this founder of Renaissance Technologies made his fortune using mathematical models, after co-developing a key concept in differential geometry — who is he?
Jim Simons (April 25, 1938 - May 10, 2024) was an American hedge fund manager, investor, mathematician, and philanthropist.
This American biologist and one-time Communist Party member had four husbands, the last being the physicist who led Los Alamos — who was she?
Kitty Oppenheimer (ne Puening; August 8, 1910 - October 27, 1972) was an American biologist, botanist, and a member of the Communist Party of America until leaving in the 1930s.
A Ming-dynasty naturalist poured 27 years into a sprawling pharmacology compendium of nearly 1,900 entries, 11,000 prescriptions, and over a thousand herbs — who was this herbalist and physician?
Li Shizhen (July 3, 1518 - 1593), courtesy name Dongbi, was a Chinese acupuncturist, herbalist, naturalist, pharmacologist, physician, and writer of the Ming dynasty.
About 90% of its cases fall into the non-Hodgkin variety, and its tell-tale signs include painless swollen lymph nodes and night sweats — which group of white-blood-cell cancers is this?
Lymphoma is a group of blood and lymph tumors that develop from lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell).

Awarded the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta, this German theoretical physicist is considered the originator of quantum theory and one of the founders of modern physics — who is he?
Max Planck (23 April 1858 - 4 October 1947) was a German theoretical physicist.
This unit of time, normally equal to 60 seconds, can rarely stretch to 61 seconds under the UTC time standard because of a leap second — what is it?
Minute (symbol: min) is a unit of time defined as equal to 60 seconds.

This European twin-engine military helicopter was the first production helicopter ever built with entirely fly-by-wire flight controls, coming in both troop-transport and naval anti-submarine variants — what aircraft is it?
NHIndustries NH90 is a medium-sized European twin-engine multi-role military helicopter.
Built from nucleotide units of a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogenous base, these biomolecules come in two main classes distinguished by whether their sugar is ribose or deoxyribose — what are they?
Nucleic acid are large biomolecules that are crucial in all cells and viruses.
Belonging to the pea family and native to Mesoamerica, this vine produces blue or white flowers and an edible tuberous root known in Spanish as jícama — which species?
Pachyrhizus erosus (from Nahuatl languages: xicamatl) or Mexican turnip, is a native Mesoamerican vine, although the name jicama most commonly refers to the plant's edible tuberous root.
This mammalian skin secretion comes in two types — a watery kind for cooling and an oilier kind found in the armpits that gains odor from bacteria — what is it?
Perspiration is the fluid secreted by sweat glands in the skin of mammals.
Known as greater plantain, this Eurasian-native flowering plant is often confused by name with a banana relative, despite no real botanical connection between the two. Which species is it?
Plantago major is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
This viscous, nearly odorless liquid with a faintly sweet taste is classified as a diol and is approved by the FDA as a safe food additive — what compound is it?
Propylene glycol (IUPAC name: propane-1,2-diol) is a viscous, colorless liquid.
This transhumanist inventor who pioneered text-to-speech and OCR technology later won the $500,000 Lemelson-MIT Prize in 2001 for his work on artificial intelligence — who is he?
Ray Kurzweil (born February 12, 1948) is an American computer scientist, author, entrepreneur, futurist, and inventor.
Born in 1858, this German inventor devised a compression-ignition engine so significant that it and its fuel now both carry his surname — who was he?
Rudolf Diesel (18 March 1858 - 29 September 1913) was a German inventor and mechanical engineer.
This bodily fluid carries reproductive cells along with fructose and enzymes that help them survive their journey toward an egg — name the fluid?
Semen is a bodily fluid that contains spermatozoa from the male gonads of animals.
A white crystalline compound most important industrially as a nitrite salt, and probably best known as a food additive in processed meats. What is it?
Sodium nitrite is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula NaNO2.

Tracing its lineage back to ancestral fish from the Early Jurassic period roughly 174 to 201 million years ago, this family of 27 fish species is one of only two living branches of an ancient order that also includes the paddlefish — name this fish family?
Sturgeon are the 27 species of fish belonging to the family Acipenseridae.
Known pharmaceutically as dronabinol, this is the principal psychoactive compound found in cannabis, used medically to relieve chemotherapy-induced nausea. What compound is it?
Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is a cannabinoid found in cannabis.
Following the instructions of the genetic code, which cellular process decodes mRNA outside the nucleus to assemble a polypeptide chain?
Translation (biology) is the process in biological cells in which proteins are produced using RNA molecules as templates.

Named after an 18th-century Italian physicist and first published in 1797, this phenomenon explains why fluid pressure drops as it speeds up through a narrower pipe section — powering wine aerators and vacuum ejectors. What is it called?
Venturi effect is the reduction in fluid pressure that results when a moving fluid speeds up as it is funneled from one section of a pipe to another, smaller section.
Chairman of the Polish People's Party since 2015 and a former Minister of Labour and Social Affairs, this physician-turned-politician ran for the Polish presidency in 2020 — who is he?
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (born 10 August 1981) is a Polish physician and politician, who has served as the Deputy Prime Minister of Poland, and Minister of National Defence since 2023.
Unearthed in Montana by Jack Horner's team in 1987, this 20-foot horned dinosaur sported a bony neck-frill and lived roughly 75 million years ago — which species?
Achelousaurus: Genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from North America.
Often called the father of theoretical computer science, this Englishman gave us a famous 'machine' that formalized the very idea of computation — who was he?

Nicknamed 'lazy eye,' this childhood vision disorder occurs when the brain favors one eye over the other, and correcting the underlying cause doesn't restore sight right away — what is this condition?
Amblyopia: Failure of the brain to process input from one eye.
Comprising over 22,000 species including ragworms, earthworms, and leeches, this phylum of segmented worms use parapodia to move — what is it?
Annelid: Phylum of segmented worms. The basic annelid form consists of multiple segments called metameres.
This pigmented ring of skin around the nipple contains sebaceous glands as well as the openings of the milk ducts — what's it called?
Areola: Pigmented area on the breast around the nipple.
The famous AL 288-1 skeleton nicknamed 'Lucy,' unearthed in Ethiopia's Afar region, belongs to which extinct East African hominin species that lived roughly 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago?
Australopithecus afarensis: Extinct hominid from the Pliocene of East Africa.
Coming on over about 48 hours, this temporary facial paralysis droops one side of the face and can heighten sensitivity to sound — what condition is it?
Bell's palsy: Facial paralysis. Bell's palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side of the face.
Rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, this deciduous shrub's glossy dark berries are cooked into jams and syrups or fermented into cassis — what is it?
Blackcurrant: Species of flowering plant in the gooseberry family Grossulariaceae.

This infraorder of decapod crustaceans tucks a stubby tail-like abdomen under a hard shell and ends its front pair of legs in pincers — over 1.5 million tonnes of them are eaten by humans yearly. What group is it?
Brachyura: Crustacean. The true crabs are the largest of the crab decapod groups with carcinised body forms.
Common in cancer, heart failure, and other serious illnesses, this syndrome causes muscle wasting that better nutrition alone can't reverse — what is it?
In 1886 this German engineer patented what's considered the first practical automobile, and his Mannheim company later merged with Daimler — who is he?
Carl Benz: German designer and engineer (1844–1929)
Documented anatomically since the time of Hippocrates over 2,000 years ago, this roughly 4-centimeter-long fibromuscular organ connects the vagina to the uterine cavity. What structure is this?
Cervix: Lower part of the uterus in the female reproductive system.
This complex of DNA and histone proteins packages long strands of genetic material into compact structures while controlling access for transcription, replication and repair — what is it?
Chromatin: Complex of DNA and protein in eukaryotic cells.

Triggered by an abnormal immune response to gluten found in wheat, barley, and rye, this chronic autoimmune condition mainly affects the small intestine and often causes malabsorption in children — which condition?
Coeliac disease: Autoimmune disorder. Coeliac disease (Commonwealth English) or celiac disease (American English) is a chronic autoimmune disease, mainly affecting the small intestine.
A heart disease involving reduced blood flow to cardiac muscle due to buildup of plaque in heart arteries — the most common cardiovascular disease. What is it?
Coronary artery disease: Reduction of blood flow to the heart. Procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) may be used in severe disease.
This closed sac in the body, distinct from an abscess of pus, forms a shell of abnormal cells and may contain air, fluid, or semi-solid material — what is it, medically?
Cyst: Closed sac growth on the body. A cyst is a closed sac in the body, having a distinct envelope and division compared with the nearby tissue.

Found in many cough and cold medicines, this morphinan-class compound was approved by the FDA in 2022 as part of a rapid-acting antidepressant combo, but can act as a dissociative hallucinogen at high doses. What substance is it?
Dextromethorphan: Cough suppressant and dissociative drug.
Sold over the counter as Unisom and combined with vitamin B6 to ease morning sickness, this first-generation antihistamine is one of the world's most widely used sleep aids — which drug?
Doxylamine: First-generation antihistamine used as a short-term sedative and hypnotic (sleep aid)
Appointed to the Supreme Court by Barack Obama in 2010, this former Harvard Law dean became the fourth woman ever to serve as a justice — who is she?
Elena Kagan: US Supreme Court justice since 2010.
A rod-shaped gut bacterium that's mostly harmless or even helpful — some strains produce vitamin K2 and fend off nastier microbes — what is its name?
Sold in Italian restaurants as branzino, this slow-growing ocean fish is the most important species farmed commercially in the Mediterranean — what fish is it?
European seabass: Species of fish. It is one of only six species in its family, Moronidae, collectively called the temperate basses.

Boldly patterned in black and yellow to warn predators of its toxicity, this European amphibian can live for more than 50 years and is now vulnerable due to an introduced fungal disease — what species is it?
Fire salamander: Species of amphibian. The fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) is a common species of salamander found in Europe.
A French economist who gave up accounting to lecture across France, he founded peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union before sharing the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. Who was he?
Frédéric Passy: French economist and pacifist (1822–1912)
Ranging from Baja California to Japan's coast, this cephalopod is the largest of its kind on Earth and a common aquarium favorite — which creature?
Giant Pacific octopus: Species of cephalopod. It can be found from the intertidal zone down to 2,000 m (6,600 ft), and is best-adapted to colder, oxygen- and nutrient-rich waters.
One of China's 'Four Great Domestic Fish,' this herbivorous freshwater species was later introduced to Europe and the US to control aquatic weeds — which fish?
Grass carp: Species of fish. This Asian carp is the only species of the genus Ctenopharyngodon.
The son of a famous physicist and his first wife, this Swiss-American engineer taught hydraulic engineering at Berkeley and became renowned for research on sediment transport — who is he?

Hans Albert Einstein: Swiss-American engineer and educator. Hans Albert Einstein (May 14, 1904 – July 26, 1973) was a Swiss-American engineer, the second child and first son of physicists Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić.

First synthesized in 1940 by chemist Roger Adams via hydrogenation of THC isomers, this psychoactive cannabis-derived compound is sold in vaporizers despite never being drug-approved — which compound?
Lightest and most abundant element in the universe, it makes up about 75% of all normal matter and fuels the stars — colorless, odorless, and highly combustible. What element is it?
Hydrogen: Chemical element with atomic number 1 (H)
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length has been pegged to exactly 25.4 millimeters since the mid-20th century — what is it?
Inch: Unit of length. The inch (symbol: in or ″) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.

The New York Times once called him "the nation's most influential evangelical leader," yet he was never an ordained minister — instead this psychologist founded Focus on the Family and led it from 1977 to 2010. Who was he?
James Dobson: American evangelical Christian psychologist and author (1936–2025)
Struggling with a morphine addiction from a Civil War saber wound, this pharmacist and chemist developed a coca-and-caffeine beverage in 1886 that became Coca-Cola — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton: American pharmacist, inventor of Coca-Cola (1831–1888)
First described in 1845 by a German physicist, these two equalities govern current and voltage in electrical networks and generalized Georg Ohm's work — what are they called?
Kirchhoff's circuit laws: Two equalities that deal with the current and potential difference.
Spread through the bite of sandflies, this parasitic disease can appear in cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral forms, the last marked by fever and an enlarged spleen — what is it called?
Leishmaniasis: Disease caused by parasites of the Leishmania type.

This catch-all name covers over 7,000 squamate species on every continent but Antarctica — from finger-length geckos to the three-meter Komodo dragon, with a few 'legless' lineages thrown in. What is it?
Found from Gibraltar to across Asia, these Old World monkeys live in troops centered on dominant matriarchs, and one Malaysian species eats about 70 rats a year — what are they?
Macaque: Genus of Old World monkeys. The macaques constitute a genus (Macaca) of gregarious Old World monkeys of the subfamily Cercopithecinae.
Prized by fur trappers for its yellowish-to-dark-brown coat, this bushy-tailed, weasel-like mammal is adapted to life in the taiga's coniferous forests — what is it?
Nicknamed 'Swallow' as a fighter and 'Storm Bird' as a bomber, this German aircraft was the world's first operational jet-powered fighter, first flying on jet power in 1942 — what was it?
Messerschmitt Me 262: First operational jet-powered fighter aircraft. The design of what would become the Me 262 started in April 1939, before World War II.
Nicknamed the 'sensitive plant,' this legume's leaves fold inward within seconds of being touched and reopen a few minutes later — what plant is it?
Mimosa pudica: Species of creeping annual plant.
This cancer attacks plasma cells — the white blood cells that normally make antibodies — often silently at first before bringing bone pain, anemia, and kidney trouble. What is it?
Multiple myeloma: Cancer of plasma cells. There is an increased risk of multiple myeloma in certain occupations, due to occupational exposure to aromatic hydrocarbon solvents.
Also called roundworms, these mostly free-living animals have a tubular digestive tract with openings at both ends and are grouped with arthropods in the clade Ecdysozoa — what are they?
This facial organ houses the nares, connects to the humidity-regulating paranasal sinuses, and serves as an alternate airway for nursing infants — which body part?
Nose: Organ that smells and facilitates breathing.
First domesticated in China's Yangtze River basin more than 8,000 years ago, this grass species is the world's most widely cultivated rice — which species?
Oryza sativa: Species of plant. Oryza sativa belongs to the genus Oryza and the BOP clade in the grass family Poaceae.
Defined as the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond, this unit equals about 3.26 light-years — which unit?
Parsec: Unit of length in astronomy.
Smaller than 3 millimetres and caused by leaking capillaries, these tiny red or purple skin spots can be forensically significant when found around the eyes or neck — what are they called?
Petechia: Small red or purple blemish on the skin, eyes, etc. due to rupture of capillaries.
This imperial and US customary unit of volume is exactly one-eighth of a gallon, though the British version is about 20% larger than its American counterpart — which unit?

Pint: Unit of volume in the imperial and US systems. The pint (symbol pt, sometimes abbreviated as p) is a unit of volume or capacity in both the imperial and United States customary measurement systems.
Also called caustic potash and written KOH, this dangerously corrosive white solid is a prototypical strong base and the key precursor to most liquid and soft soaps — which compound?
Potassium hydroxide: Inorganic compound (KOH). It has many industrial and niche applications, most of which utilize its caustic nature and its reactivity toward acids.

Harvested from Plantago seeds mainly grown in northern India, this dietary fiber relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and can modestly lower cholesterol and blood pressure with regular use. What is it?
Psyllium: Plant used as a dietary fiber.
This genus of muroid rodents gives its scientific name to the common rat, though not every animal called a rat actually belongs to it — which genus?
Sold under the brand name Rituxan, this monoclonal antibody treats non-Hodgkin lymphoma, rheumatoid arthritis and several other autoimmune conditions via slow IV infusion — what is it?
Named after a 19th-century American veterinary surgeon, this genus of rod-shaped, flagella-covered bacteria includes over 2,650 serotypes divided among just two species — what is it?
Salmonella: Genus of bacteria. Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, (bacillus) Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae.

Caused by a sudden burst of synchronized electrical activity in the brain, this neurological event affects roughly 50 million people worldwide and can range from a brief blank stare to a full convulsion — what is it?
Seizure: Period of symptoms due to excessive or synchronous neuronal brain activity.
This structural framework supporting an animal's body can take the form of a rigid outer shell, an internal bony frame, or simply fluid pressure inside the body. What is it?
Skeleton: Part of the body that forms the supporting structure.

First described in 1915 by a German paleontologist from Egyptian fossils that were destroyed during World War II, this dinosaur genus wasn't represented by new material until the early 2000s — which genus?
Spinosaurus: Genus of spinosaurid dinosaur. The genus was known first from Egyptian remains discovered in 1912 and described by German palaeontologist Ernst Stromer in 1915.
The first variable-sweep-wing aircraft to enter Soviet service, this fighter-bomber was produced from 1967 to 1990 and exported in variants flown across the Arab world — which jet?
Sukhoi Su-17: Soviet variable-sweep wing fighter-bomber. The Sukhoi Su-17 (Russian: Су-17; NATO reporting name: Fitter) is a variable-sweep wing fighter-bomber developed for the Soviet military.
The lone living family within its primate infraorder, these small Southeast Asian mammals favor forests thick with liana vines, which give them vertical support as they climb — which animal?
In tetrapods this body region between the neck and abdomen houses the heart, lungs, and thymus gland, while in insects and crustaceans it forms one of three main body segments — what is it called?
Thorax: Frontal part of an animal's body, between its head and abdomen.
Approved in the US in 1981, this sedating antidepressant from the SARI class racked up more than 24 million prescriptions in 2023, making it the fifth most common antidepressant — what is it?
Trazodone: Antidepressant medication. Trazodone is an antidepressant medication used to treat major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and insomnia.
Roughly 20 to 30 centimeters long in adults, this smooth-muscle tube carries urine from each kidney down to the bladder — what is it called?
Ureter: Tubes used in the urinary system in most animals.
Known as the 'true foxes,' animals in this genus are smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, with a signature dark triangular mask between the eyes — which genus?
Vulpes: Genus of true foxes. The members of this genus are colloquially referred to as true foxes, meaning they form a proper clade.
Made up of eight carpal bones and home to the carpal tunnel and the anatomical snuff box, this joint connects the hand to the forearm — which body part?
Wrist: Part of the arm between the lower arm and the hand.
The symbol for carbon is C. Carbon is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
What is the chemical symbol for hafnium?
The symbol for hafnium is Hf. Hafnium is a chemical element; it has symbol Hf and atomic number 72.

In what year was Farrah Fawcett born?
Farrah Fawcett: Mary Ferrah Leni "Farrah" Fawcett (February 2, 1947 – June 25, 2009) was an American actress.
In what year was Angelina Jolie born?
Angelina Jolie ( joh-LEE; born Angelina Jolie Voight [ VOYT] on June 4, 1975) is an American actress, filmmaker, and humanitarian.
In what year was Viggo Mortensen born?
Viggo Mortensen: Viggo Peter Mortensen Jr. (Danish: [ˈviko ˈmɒːtn̩sn̩]; born October 20, 1958) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Marisa Tomei born?
Marisa Tomei (Italian: [toˈmɛi]; born December 4, 1964) is an American actress.
In what year was Steve Carell born?
Steve Carell: Steven John Carell (born August 16, 1962) is an American actor and comedian.
In what year was Natasha Lyonne born?
Natasha Lyonne: Natasha Bianca Lyonne Braunstein ( lee-OHN; born April 4, 1979) is an American actress, director, comedian, producer, writer, and tech executive.

Jason Bateman: Jason Kent Bateman (born January 14, 1969) is an American actor.

Ryuichi Sakamoto: With his YMO bandmates Haruomi Hosono and Yukihiro Takahashi, Sakamoto influenced and pioneered a number of electronic music genres.
In what year was Han So-hee born?
Han So-hee: Lee So-hee (Korean: 이소희; born November 18, 1993), better known by the stage name Han So-hee (한소희), is a South Korean actress.
In what year was Hugh Laurie born?
Hugh Laurie: James Hugh Calum Laurie (born 11 June 1959) is an English actor, comedian, and musician.
In what year was Luke Evans born?
Luke Evans: Luke George Evans (born 15 April 1979) is a Welsh actor and singer.
In what year did Gene Hackman die?
Gene Hackman: Eugene Allen Hackman (January 30, 1930 – February 18, 2025) was an American actor.
In what year did Sage Stallone die?
Sage Stallone: Sage Moonblood Stallone (May 5, 1976 – July 13, 2012) was an American actor.
